Electric car sales in Eastland

In 2020, only 2 per cent of new cars sold in Eastland were electric. By 2025 this figure had risen to 15 per cent, thanks to lower prices and government payments to buyers.

Experts predict that electric cars will make up 50 per cent of new car sales by 2032. The government plans to stop the sale of new petrol cars completely in 2040.

However, there are still problems. At present, the country has only 3,000 public charging points, and most of them are in the capital. The government has promised to build 20,000 more by 2030, especially along main roads, so that drivers can make long journeys without worrying about their batteries.

groups.instructions: You are going to listen to a dialogue between a radio presenter and a woman who has sailed alone around the world. For questions 41-46 decide which of the choices A, B, C, D or E is the correct answer. You have 45 seconds to look through the questions before you listen. You will listen twice only, so listen carefully. /6 x 2 = 12 points/
groups.context:
Presenter: Welcome to 'Brave Voices'. My guest is Lucy Grant, who has just sailed alone around the world. Lucy, congratulations!
Lucy: Thank you very much.
Presenter: How long did the journey take?
Lucy: Two hundred and sixty days. I left from Plymouth, in England, at the end of March and came back in December. I was hoping to finish in two hundred days, but the weather was terrible in the Southern Ocean.
Presenter: What was the most difficult moment?
Lucy: About halfway, south of Australia, a huge wave hit the boat and broke the mast. I couldn't sail properly for days.
Presenter: What did you do?
Lucy: First, I made sure I was safe and the boat wasn't taking in water. Then I sent a message to my support team. They told me how to build a small temporary mast from the broken pieces. It took me three days, but it worked, and I sailed slowly to a port in New Zealand for repairs.
Presenter: Weren't you lonely?
Lucy: Sometimes. I spoke to my family by satellite phone once a week, and I listened to lots of audiobooks. And the albatrosses kept me company. They followed the boat for days!
Presenter: What did you learn?
Lucy: That panic never helps. If you stay calm and solve one problem at a time, you can deal with almost anything.
Presenter: Lucy Grant, thank you.

passages.title: The Mother of Trees
passages.text:
In the early 1970s, Wangari Maathai noticed that something was going wrong in her home country, Kenya. Rivers that she remembered from her childhood were drying up, forests were being cut down, and women in the countryside had to walk farther and farther every day to find firewood and clean water. Many families could no longer grow enough food.

Maathai was not an ordinary woman. She was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate degree, and she taught at the University of Nairobi. She believed that the answer to many of these problems was simple: plant trees. Trees would protect the soil, keep water in the ground and give people wood and fruit.

In 1977 she started the Green Belt Movement. The idea was to pay village women a small amount of money for every young tree they planted that survived. At first, many people laughed at her. Some officials thought that women without education could not do such work. But the women proved them wrong. They collected seeds, grew young trees in small nurseries and planted them across the country.

Maathai's work was not always easy. She often criticised the government when it tried to sell public forests and parks to builders, and she was arrested several times. Yet she never gave up. Over the following decades, the women of the Green Belt Movement planted tens of millions of trees.

In 2004, Maathai became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Some people were surprised that **it** was given for planting trees. Maathai explained that peace depends on how we share and protect the Earth's resources. She believed that when people plant trees, they also plant hope for the future.
